maraapunisaurus:enwiki:4.title: Maraapunisaurus (Disappearance of the specimen and quarry)

facts.statement: The species was originally named Amphicoelias fragillimus by Cope in 1878.
facts.quote: synonyms: Amphicoelias fragillimus Cope, 1878

facts.statement: The species was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878.
facts.quote: authority: (Cope, 1878)

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic,

facts.statement: It is a sauropod dinosaur found in the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of western North America.
facts.quote: Maraapunisaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of western North America.

facts.statement: The largest historical estimate placed its length at 58 meters and mass at 150 tonnes.
facts.quote: the largest estimate M. fragillimus to have been the longest known animal at 58 m in length with a mass of 150 tonne.

facts.statement: It possesses the tallest and largest neural spine of any animal, measuring 2.7 meters.
facts.quote: Maraapunisaurus also has the tallest and largest neural spine out of any animal (2.7 m).

facts.statement: The only known specimen was collected by Oramel William Lucas in 1877.
facts.quote: The holotype and only known specimen of Maraapunisaurus fragillimus was collected by Oramel William Lucas, shortly after he had been hired as a fossil collector by the renowned paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope, in 1877.

facts.statement: The holotype is a partial vertebra discovered in Garden Park, north of Cañon City, Colorado.
facts.quote: Lucas discovered a partial vertebra (the neural arch including the spine) of a new sauropod species in Garden Park, north of Cañon City, Colorado

facts.statement: The preserved parts measured about 1.5 meters in height, while the original height might have reached 2.7 meters.
facts.quote: The preserved parts perhaps measured 1.5 m in height; its original height might have been as tall as 2.7 m.

facts.statement: The genus name means 'huge reptile', derived from the Southern Ute word for 'huge'.
facts.quote: Maraapunisaurus means 'huge reptile' based on maraapuni, the Southern Ute for 'huge'.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter proposed a scenario for the disappearance of the specimen in 2006.
facts.quote: Kenneth Carpenter, in 2006, presented a possible scenario for the disappearance of the specimen.

facts.statement: Attempts to relocate the quarry using ground-penetrating radar failed because the bones had the same density as the surrounding rock.
facts.quote: The attempt failed because the fossilized mudstone bones were the same density as the surrounding rock, making it impossible to differentiate between the two.

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that the size of the Maraapunisaurus vertebra has been overestimated and that earlier scientists accepted the measurements without sufficient skepticism.
facts.quote: Cary Woodruff and John R. Foster concluded that the vertebra's size has been overestimated and that modern paleontologists were accepting Cope's interpretation without due skepticism.

facts.statement: A hypothesis suggests that the reported measurement of 1500 mm for the vertebra is a typographical error for 1050 mm.
facts.quote: Woodruff and Foster offer the hypothesis that the reported measurement of 1500 mm is likely a typographical error for 1050 mm.

facts.statement: Researcher Carpenter believes it is unlikely that the surveyor Lucas was merely repeating Cope's measurements, supporting the original size estimates.
facts.quote: Carpenter considers it unlikely he would have been merely re-stating what Cope had said.

facts.statement: The species was reclassified as a rebbachisaurid, leading to the creation of the new genus name Maraapunisaurus.
facts.quote: Considering it to be a rebbachisaurid upon his re-examination, the species could not be referred to the genus Amphicoelias, and so he gave it a new generic name, Maraapunisaurus.

facts.statement: The fossil was discovered during the Bone Wars, a period of intense rivalry between paleontologists Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: The discovery took place during the Bone Wars, and Cope's rival Marsh, who was "ever ready to humiliate" Cope, never called the claims into question.

facts.statement: The genus name Maraapunisaurus combines the Southern Ute word for "huge" with the Greek word for "reptile".
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Southern Ute word "Ma-ra-pu-ni", meaning "huge", and the Latinised Greek saurus, meaning reptile.

facts.statement: The classification of the specimen as a rebbachisaurid was first conjectured by an online enthusiast named Zachary Armstrong in 2014, four years before the official scientific publication.
facts.quote: Apparently, Carpenter was inspired by work of paleontology enthusiasts posted on the website DeviantArt; one user, Zachary Armstrong, known as "palaeozoologist" on the website, conjectured the same classification in 2014, four years before Carpenter's publication.

facts.statement: Based on Cope's original description, the femur of M. fragillimus was estimated to be 3.6 meters tall.
facts.quote: Cope stated that in other sauropod dinosaurs, specifically Amphicoelias altus and Camarasaurus supremus, the femora were always twice as tall as the tallest dorsal (back) vertebra, and estimated the size of an M. fragillimus femur to be 3.6 m tall.

facts.statement: Even the lowest length estimates for M. fragillimus were higher than those of Supersaurus (32.5 m), Sauroposeidon (34 m), and Argentinosaurus (30 m).
facts.quote: Carpenter pointed out that even the lowest length estimates for A. fragillimus were higher than those for other giant sauropods, such as the diplodocid Supersaurus (32.5 m), the brachiosaurid Sauroposeidon (34 m), and the titanosaur Argentinosaurus (30 m).

facts.statement: If recent estimations of Bruhathkayosaurus are accurate, Maraapunisaurus would have been the second largest land animal and the fourth largest animal overall.
facts.quote: Nevertheless, if the recent estimations of Bruhathkayosaurus were any indication, Maraapunisaurus would have been the second largest animal to walk the earth and the fourth largest animal overall.

facts.statement: In 2018, Carpenter reclassified the species as a basal member of Rebbachisauridae and renamed it Maraapunisaurus, derived from a Southern Ute word meaning "huge".
facts.quote: In 2018, Carpenter concluded from a qualitative anatomical comparison that the species was a basal member of the Rebbachisauridae, and assigned it the new name Maraapunisaurus, after a Southern Ute word maraapuni meaning "huge".

facts.statement: The basal position of Maraapunisaurus is indicated by the presence of a hyposphene, a trait shared with Histriasaurus, Comahuesaurus, and Demandasaurus.
facts.quote: The basal position would be indicated by the presence of a hyposphene, a secondary rear articulation process, which is a trait shared with the basal rebbachisaurids Histriasaurus, Comahuesaurus and Demandasaurus.

facts.statement: If Maraapunisaurus is a rebbachisaurid, it would be the oldest known member of that group and the only one discovered from the Jurassic period.
facts.quote: If Maraapunisaurus belongs to Rebbachisauridae, it would be the oldest member of its group known and the only one discovered from the Jurassic.

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus would be the only known rebbachisaurid discovered from North America.
facts.quote: It would also be the only one from North America.

facts.statement: Larger animals have longer digestive systems that retain food for longer periods, allowing them to survive on lower-quality food sources.
facts.quote: Since larger animals have longer digestive systems, food is kept in digestion for significantly longer periods of time, allowing large animals to survive on lower-quality food sources.

facts.statement: Size estimates of M. fragillimus must be treated with caution due to the lack of specimens and detailed documentation.
facts.quote: Any size estimate of M. fragillimus must be regarded with caution because of the lack of specimens and detailed, accurate documentation of its fossils.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the original description of M. fragillimus contains critical typographical errors.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that it contains potentially critical typographical errors, but this idea has been disputed.

facts.statement: Carpenter's 2018 reclassification of the taxon as a rebbachisaurid resulted in significantly different size estimates compared to earlier diplodocid classifications.
facts.quote: When Carpenter redescribed the taxon as a rebbachisaurid instead of a diplodocid in 2018, he made new, very different, size estimates.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul noted the possibility that Maraapunisaurus had more typical sauropod body proportions than previously estimated.
facts.quote: He also said that there was the possibility that Maraapunisaurus had more typical body proportions for a sauropod.

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus lived in a savanna-like environment similar to those of modern giant herbivores.
facts.quote: The environment of Maraapunisaurus was essentially a savanna, similar to the arid environments in which modern giant herbivores are found

facts.statement: Researcher Carpenter argued that Maraapunisaurus could consume ferns as a major part of its diet because its digestive system was adapted to process low-quality food.
facts.quote: Carpenter argued that the sauropod digestive system, well adapted to handle low-quality food, allows for the consumption of ferns as a large part of the sauropod diet

facts.statement: Evidence of trees 20 to 30 meters tall has been found in the environment where Maraapunisaurus lived.
facts.quote: the occasional presence of large petrified logs indicate the presence of 20 – 30 m tall trees

facts.statement: Carpenter speculated that Maraapunisaurus may have used gallery forests for shade during the day and fed on the open savanna at night.
facts.quote: Carpenter speculated that giant herbivores like Maraapunisaurus may have used the shade of the gallery forests to stay cool during the day, and done most of their feeding on the open savanna at night

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus belongs to the parent group Rebbachisauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Rebbachisauridae

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus is classified in the family Rebbachisauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Rebbachisauridae

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: Maraapunisaurus lived during the Tithonian stage, from 149.2 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tithonian to Tithonian (149.2 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Maraapunisaurus has been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the diet of sauropods: Engelmann et al. (2004) dismissed ferns as a food source due to low caloric content, while Carpenter argued that their digestive systems allowed them to consume ferns as a major part of their diet.
facts.quote: Engelmann et al. (2004) dismissed ferns as a sauropod food source due to their relatively low caloric content, Carpenter argued that the sauropod digestive system, well adapted to handle low-quality food, allows for the consumption of ferns as a large part of the sauropod diet
